add.issue.name: epiq skill: each session boots its own MCP server, so assumed identities do not mix

edit.description.md:
`epiq_actor_assume` binds the identity to the server process it is called on. Two sessions sharing one server, or a session sharing the user's own instance, would sign every write with whichever name was assumed last, and the log would merge them into one contributor.

Add a rule to the skill: every session runs its own epiq MCP instance — the one Claude Code spawns for the session, or one the agent boots itself when that failed to connect — never one shared with another session or with the user. After any restart of that instance the name has to be assumed again.

add.issue.name: epiq_issue_get should carry the ticket's comments — reading one thread costs the whole state today

edit.description.md:
The skill says to read a ticket's comments before starting, and no tool serves them. `epiq_issue_get` returns title, description, tags and assignees; the only place a comment appears is `epiq_state_get`, which is every node with its full log plus the entire event log. Reading one thread on this board today meant a 4,222-event payload.

Add `comments` to the `epiq_issue_get` response: id, author name, time and body, in log order, deleted ones omitted. Attachments alongside if the same read yields them.

add.issue.name: epiq_issue_list: filter by lane, tag, assignee and text, and a brief shape without descriptions

edit.description.md:
Answering "what is in Ongoing" or "which tickets carry from-review" means listing every open ticket with its full description and filtering client-side. On this board that is 134 tickets, most of them several paragraphs: the description is the bulk of the payload and rarely what a list is read for.

Add `swimlaneId`, `tag`, `assignee` and `query` filters, and `brief: true` returning id, ref, title, swimlane title, tag names and assignee names only. The tool description should point agents at `brief` for scanning and `epiq_issue_get` for one ticket.

add.issue.name: Plan: a Stats tab on every ticket — code quality as a triage instrument

edit.description.md:
Design ticket. The **code** side of per-ticket stats, next to `WF435EW` (event-log side) and absorbing `WHK3PN0` (patch coverage). A fifth tab beside Overview / Comments / Commits / Log.

## Why

Reviewers are retreating from reading diffs. The tab's job is not to score a ticket — it is to answer **"how hard should I look at this diff, and where"**. So: no composite quality score (it invites gaming and hides which input moved), every number carries a denominator or a repo baseline, and absence of data reads as *unknown*, never as zero.

## Verified by prototype, not guessed

Ran the whole pipeline over three real tickets on this repo:

| ref | commits | files | +/- | test:code | comment % | patch coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `4Z33DKP` | 6 | 16 | +3624 / -1894 | 0.63 | 6.1% | 43/46 (93%) |
| `5ZCMF7C` | 6 | 15 | +6686 / -5584 | 0.00 | 6.6% | 731/861 (85%) |
| `MBB6WY5` | 1 | 2 | +159 / -19 | 1.61 | 12.2% | 29/29 (100%) |

84ms to scan six commits' patches, 34-221ms for blame. Cheap enough to compute on tab open.

**Two findings that decide the design:**

1. **Anchor coverage with `git blame`, not with diff line numbers.** Matching the diff's added line numbers against lcov and guarding staleness with "has a later commit touched this file?" — what `WHK3PN0` proposes — discarded the whole file on `MBB6WY5` and reported `0/0`. Blaming HEAD and keeping the lines whose sha is one of the ticket's own maps the ticket's code to *current* line numbers, so drift is handled rather than thrown away: `0/0` -> `29/29`. Free second stat: **code survival** — 2962 of `5ZCMF7C`'s 6686 added lines still stand at HEAD.
2. **A lone coverage percentage would lie.** On `4Z33DKP`, 1889 added lines sit in files the report has never heard of (`.tsx`, not in the unit suite) and 242 more in instrumented files with no `DA` record (types, braces, blanks). 46 lines were actually measured. Every line needs one of four states — **covered / uncovered / not instrumented / not in the report** — and the denominator goes on screen. "93%" alone is worse than no number.

## The catalogue

**Change shape** (free, `git log --numstat`): files, +/-, net, commits, directories spanned, new/deleted files, concentration (share of the change in its largest file), **self-churn** (lines the ticket wrote then rewrote in a later commit — thrash), **survival at HEAD**.

**Tests**: test-lines vs code-lines, *did it touch a test at all* (badge), **tests deleted**, **`.skip` / `.only` added** (`.only` silently disables the rest of a suite — the best catch on this list), patch coverage as above, repo total + report age.

**Comments & docs**: comment share of added non-blank lines **compared to the repo's baseline for that language** — the deviation is the signal; the absolute number is noise and "more comments" as a target is Goodhart bait. Companions: TODO/FIXME/HACK added vs removed, **commented-out code** (a comment line that parses like code), docs touched.

**Languages**: extension -> language over changed lines, split test vs code, plus *new language introduced to the repo by this ticket*.

**Hygiene flags** (binary badges, a line of scanning each): lockfile/generated/vendor touched, binary or large file added, **dependencies added** (`package.json`/`go.mod`/`Cargo.toml`/`requirements.txt`), CI/Dockerfile/build touched, debug prints added, max indentation depth added (an honest language-agnostic stand-in for nesting, *not* "cyclomatic complexity"), duplicate added blocks within the change.

**Git-history risk** (what a diff cannot tell you): **hotspot** (how often these files changed in 90 days, by how many authors), **age of the code modified** (blame dates of deleted lines), **change coupling** (files that historically travel with these and were *not* touched here — the best single review pointer here), bus factor.

**Review signals**: diff comments on the ticket, tickets filed from its diff, review progress. That last is `localStorage` today (`reviewed-files.ts`, keyed `sha:path`, per browser) so it cannot answer "has anyone reviewed this" — its own ticket.

**Not in scope**: a composite score; real complexity metrics (needs per-language parsers); comment count as a target.

## Shape

`source/lib/stats/` — pure, Node-side, one implementation for GUI/MCP/TUI, as `WF435EW` already proposed:

- `patch-scan.ts` — one `git show --unified=0` spawn for *all* the ticket's shas, parsed to added/removed lines with line numbers
- `languages.ts`, `comment-density.ts`, `flags.ts`
- `coverage/` — discovery + one parser per format
- `blame-anchor.ts`, `hotspots.ts`

`issue:stats:get` / `issue:stats:result` wrapped by `issueId`, exactly like `issue:commits:get`. `epiq_issue_stats` MCP over the same function — the agents writing this code should be able to read their own readout. `'stats'` added to `IssueDetailsTab` + `?tab=stats` + `IssueStats.tsx`. Cache keyed by ref + sha set + report mtime, like `FULL_TIMELINE_CACHE`. Caps like `MAX_DIFF_FILES_FOR_DATA`, degrading to numstat-only with a note.

## Coverage: the answers to WHK3PN0

- **Format**: lcov first. Istanbul JSON, Cobertura, JaCoCo and Go coverprofiles all parse with plain string scanning and no new dependency, so more formats is cheap follow-on, not a fork.
- **Discovery**: conventional paths (`coverage/`, `htmlcov/`, `target/site/jacoco/`, `.nyc_output/`) with an explicit override in a committed `.epiq/stats.json`. Nothing found = no coverage section, nothing enforced.
- **Staleness**: report mtime vs the file's last commit, shown as an age; blame anchoring does the real work.

## Seams to be honest about

- A commit links only if its subject carries the ref, so **"no commits" is not "no work"** — same caveat `WF435EW` raises.
- Git author is always the repo user here and AI trailers are stripped before merge, so **human-vs-agent authorship cannot come from git** — only from the ticket's assignee in the event log.
- Blame counts *surviving* lines, so a ticket whose code was later rewritten under-reports. Show both: lines added, and lines still standing.

add.issue.name: Stats: comment density against a repo baseline, and the hygiene flags

edit.description.md:
From `6YRCWTM`.

`comment-density.ts` — a line classifier per language family (`//`, `#`, `/* */`, `"""`, `<!-- -->`), run over the added lines. Deliberately line-based and approximate; say so in the UI rather than pretending to lex.

**Show it against the repo's own baseline for that language, never bare.** "6% here, 11% across the repo" is a question worth asking; "6%" alone is a number to game. Prototype: `4Z33DKP` 6.1%, `MBB6WY5` 12.2%.

- TODO/FIXME/HACK/XXX added vs removed
- commented-out code — a comment line that parses like code
- debug prints added (`console.log`, `debugger`, `print(`, `fmt.Println`)
- dependencies added (`package.json`, `go.mod`, `Cargo.toml`, `requirements.txt`)
- lockfile/generated/vendor touched, binary or large file added, CI/Dockerfile/build touched

add.issue.name: Stats: lcov discovery and blame-anchored patch coverage

edit.description.md:
The coverage section of `6YRCWTM`. Supersedes the mechanism sketched in `WHK3PN0`; that ticket's three open questions are answered there.

**Discovery**: lcov only to start. Conventional paths (`coverage/`, `htmlcov/`, `target/site/jacoco/`, `.nyc_output/`) plus an explicit override in a committed `.epiq/stats.json`. Nothing found means no coverage section — nothing enforced, nothing inferred.

**Anchoring — the part that matters.** Do *not* match the diff's added line numbers against the report and drop a file that later commits touched: on `MBB6WY5` that guard reported `0/0`. Instead `git blame --line-porcelain HEAD` each touched file and keep the lines whose sha is one of the ticket's own. That maps the ticket's code to *current* line numbers, so drift is handled rather than discarded — `0/0` becomes `29/29`. Cost measured at 34-221ms per ticket.

Free second stat from the same blame: **code survival** — 2962 of `5ZCMF7C`'s 6686 added lines still stand at HEAD. Show both, since blame only sees surviving lines and would otherwise quietly under-report a rewritten ticket.

**Four states per line, and the denominator on screen**: covered / uncovered / not instrumented / not in the report. On `4Z33DKP`, 1889 added lines are in files the report never heard of and 242 more have no `DA` record; 46 were actually measured. A bare "93%" is worse than no number.

Also show the report's age (mtime vs the file's last commit) and the repo total it carries.

add.issue.name: Stats: the git-history risk section — hotspots, code age, change coupling

edit.description.md:
The part of `6YRCWTM` a diff cannot answer on its own. Loads lazily, behind the sections that are instant.

- **Hotspot** — how often each touched file changed in the last 90 days, and by how many authors. One `git log --since --name-only`, counted.
- **Age of the code being modified** — blame dates of the deleted lines. Rewriting last week's code is not rewriting 2019's, and the tab currently cannot tell them apart.
- **Change coupling** — files that historically travel with these and were *not* touched here. The best single review pointer in the whole plan: it names the thing somebody forgot.
- **Bus factor** of the touched files.

Each is a comparison against the repo's own history, so it needs no configuration and works in any language.

add.issue.name: The ticket narrowing switches itself back on when a re-render lands between the change and its URL

edit.description.md:
Unticking "Ticket only" can silently fail: the box goes back to ticked and `?ticket=1` reappears in the URL. Caught by `5NPENPY`'s own e2e ("it follows to the next ticket rather than being cancelled by it") failing in a loaded pre-push run, where it looked like a flake — it passes on a quiet machine.

Not a test problem. `useBoardSelection` carries four values a route change would otherwise drop (`offset`, `zoom`, `windowOnly`, `ticketOnly`) in a ref, written during render from the selection it derives off `searchParams`. Writing a change is therefore two steps: the ref first, then the URL a render later.

Any unrelated re-render landing between those two steps still reads the pre-change query. It recomputes the selection from `ticket=1`, and the render-phase write puts `ticketOnly: true` straight back over the change. The bare query then arrives, `hasSelectionParams` is false, so the selection falls back to the carried values — now reverted — and the effect writes `ticket=1` back into the address bar. The narrowing puts itself back on, exactly what the ref's own comment says it exists to prevent.

A `timeline` message off the socket is enough to be that re-render, so this is reachable in normal use and not only under test load; a busy machine just widens the window.

Fix: key the carried values to the query they were read out of, so a render still holding the pre-change query is recognised as having nothing newer to say and leaves them alone. Compared as a string, since react-router can hand back a fresh `URLSearchParams` for the same query.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: the carried values now travel with the query they were read out of — `SelectionCarry = {query, values}` in `board-selection.ts`, with `carryRender` and `carryChange` as the only two ways it moves.

`carryRender` is what a render offers; it returns the carry unchanged when the query matches the one already held, so the render that lands between a change and its URL is recognised as having nothing newer to say. `carryChange` is what a change writes ahead of the URL, and deliberately keeps the *old* query as the key, since those values are precisely the ones superseding it. Compared as a string rather than by identity, because react-router 7 can hand back a fresh `URLSearchParams` for the same query — in which case the `useMemo` recomputes from the stale query and clobbers just the same, so identity comparison would have fixed only half of it.

Pure functions rather than logic inside the hook, so the race is a unit test instead of an e2e that only fails on a loaded machine. Four cases in `board-selection.test.ts`, the key one replaying render `ticket=1` → change to `ticketOnly: false` → stale re-render on the old query → the bare query landing. Verified red before green: with the guard removed it fails `expected true to be false`, the same symptom as the browser.

`useBoardSelection` got shorter on the way — the inline `CarriedKey` type and both hand-rolled field copies are gone.

add.issue.name: Coverage history: snapshot a ticket's own numbers as an event, not the report

edit.description.md:
Falls out of `WB7RVPX`. A coverage report is whatever the last test run left on disk, so the Stats tab can only ever answer about *now*. Worth separating the two questions, because only one of them needs history:

- **"Is the code this ticket wrote tested?"** — a live property of the codebase. Today's report plus blame anchoring answers it exactly, and it degrades honestly: lines that no longer exist drop out of the denominator, and the report's age is on screen. Already built, needs nothing.
- **"Was it tested when it landed?"** — a historical fact, and one git cannot reconstruct: coverage is not derivable from source. It needs a measurement taken at the time.

For triage — which is what the tab is for — the first is the question that matters. The second is what this ticket is about.

## The cheap shape

Do **not** store reports. An lcov file is ~260 KB per run and, on the state branch, permanent and replicated to every clone. What is actually needed is a hundred bytes: this ticket's own covered / uncovered / not-instrumented / not-in-report counts, the HEAD sha, the report's path and mtime, and who took it.

That is an event like any other — it appends, it replicates, it time-travels, and no later edit changes it. The tab then shows both numbers and the gap between them is itself the interesting part: coverage decaying as other people edit the file is invisible today.

Taken by an explicit call (`epiq_stats_snapshot`) from CI after the test run, or on ticket close. Never automatically on read: a stat that writes to the log when somebody opens a tab would fill the log with duplicates of itself.

Open, and why this is tagged for you:

- It is a second new event type, alongside `WCJXWAE`. Both should be decided together rather than one at a time — read `epiq-architecture` first.
- Several snapshots of one ticket are a series, not a conflict, so ordering is the standard story. But "which snapshot does the tab show" is a choice: the newest, or the one nearest the ticket's last commit.
- No snapshot must read as **never measured**, never as zero.

add.issue.name: Public mode: let the GUI server be reachable from outside loopback

edit.description.md:
The GUI server is loopback-only by construction, which is right for the local tool and fatal for anything hosted. Four edges refuse a browser that reaches it through a proxy:

- `server.listen(port, '127.0.0.1')` is hardcoded (`source/gui/api/api-server.ts:204`).
- `isForeignOrigin` accepts only `http:` on a loopback host whose port equals the bound port (`source/gui/api/lib/origin-guard.ts:21`), so behind HTTPS it refuses every write *and* the websocket handshake.
- The client builds `ws://${window.location.host}/ws` (`source/gui/client/lib/use-board-socket.ts:101`), which is mixed content on an HTTPS page — the socket never opens.
- `project:open` and `sync` are reachable by anyone on the port; neither belongs in a public sandbox.

Add an opt-in public mode, entirely through env, leaving every default exactly as it is today:

- `EPIQ_GUI_HOST` — bind address, default `127.0.0.1`.
- `EPIQ_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` — when set, that exact origin also passes the guard, and `https:` is permitted.
- `EPIQ_PUBLIC_MODE=1` — refuse `project:open` and `sync` at the websocket router.
- The client's socket scheme follows the page: `wss:` when `location.protocol === 'https:'`.

Unset, behaviour must be byte-identical to today: loopback, `http:`, port equality. The origin guard's own tests are the place that has to say so.

add.issue.name: A static demo board for the landing page, built in the pipeline and served from ghpages

edit.description.md:
A "try it" link on the landing page that opens a real, clickable epiq board — no install, no server, no account. The point is adoption: epiq's argument is visual, and right now you have to clone and run before you can see it.

Served as static files from ghpages, which means the board has to run entirely in the browser. That is more feasible than it sounds, because the transport is already the only seam: the client speaks a closed set of websocket messages (`source/gui/api/lib/websocket.model.ts`) and knows nothing else about the server.

What the exploration found:

- The replay core is already node-free — `event-boot.ts`, `event-materialize.ts`, `timeline-index.ts`, `api/issues.ts`, `api/issue-projection.ts` and `api/state.ts` (`getGuiState`) import no node builtins.
- `state.ts` and `node-builder.ts` are clean too; `state.ts` reaches the filesystem in exactly one place (lines 115-120, `resolveClosestEpiqProjectRoot` + `readProjectFile`), which is a single injection point rather than a rewrite.
- Only the I/O leaves are node-bound: `event-load.ts`, `event-persist.ts`, `log-signature.ts`, `storage/paths.ts`, `project-setup.ts`.
- `epiq-time-travel.ts` is node- and git-bound, but the part that matters for a demo — replaying the log to a moment — sits on the pure side.

So the work is:

1. A browser entry that implements the websocket message protocol in-memory instead of over a socket.
2. Stub the one or two filesystem leaf call sites.
3. Ship a seeded event log as a static asset, plus pre-baked JSON for the git-backed views (`commits:get`, `commit:diff:get`, `issue:commits:get`) — the demo repo's commits are fixed, so they can be baked rather than computed.
4. Build it in the pipeline and publish alongside the landing page; link it from there.

Board time travel replays client-side and stays live, which is the feature worth demoing. Edits live in memory and vanish on reload — acceptable, provided the UI says so rather than letting someone think their board was lost.

Note the standing constraint this runs into head-on: client code must not import `source/lib/event/*` today, because those modules drag in node builtins and break `npm run build:gui`. This ticket is partly about making that boundary crossable for the pure modules.

The demo seed must be synthetic. Exporting the real board would publish contributor names, emails and internal ticket text to a public, cached, hard-to-retract site.

Guardrail against drift: a demo that behaves subtly unlike epiq is worse than no demo. Build it from the same client bundle and run the existing Playwright suite against the static build.

add.issue.name: Lint rule: no raw control characters in source

edit.description.md:
Bit twice in one session, both in `6YRCWTM`'s work: a raw NUL byte written into a template literal (`flags.ts`, then `epiq-issue-stats.ts`) where an escape was meant.

Why it matters more than it looks. Git classifies a file containing NUL as **binary**: no diff, no blame, no GitHub review of that file, from then on. `epiq-issue-stats.ts` reached a pull request as `Bin 0 -> 3009 bytes`. `grep` also treats the file as binary and silently returns nothing, so searching for the very line you are looking at finds it missing — which is how the second one was found, by accident.

Neither prettier nor tsc says a word: both are valid string contents.

`no-control-regex` is not this — it covers regexes only. What is wanted is a rule over source text: no character below U+0020 other than tab and newline, escapes (`\0`, `\x1e`) being fine since they are ASCII in the file. `no-irregular-whitespace` is a near neighbour and does not cover it.

Cheapest version if a rule is awkward: a check in the pre-commit hook over the staged diff.

edit.title.name: A public epiq demo: what it would take, and why it is parked

edit.description.md:
Explored hosting a live epiq that people can reach and click, to lower the bar to trying it. Parked — findings kept so the question does not need re-exploring.

## Verdict: not now

Three reasons, in order of weight:

1. **A synthetic board undersells the product.** epiq's argument is that it is welded to *your* repo's real history. A demo board of fake tickets and fake contributors removes exactly what makes it compelling; `npx epiq` on your own repo is the better demo and already exists.
2. **Trying it is not the bottleneck.** For a tool installed with `npx`, friction-to-try is near zero and every potential user already has a git repo with history. Pre-traction tools fail on awareness and comprehension, which a demo does not move.
3. **A shim is a permanent tax on a marketing asset.** It is a second implementation of the transport, on the critical path of every future protocol change, and a demo that behaves subtly unlike epiq is worse than none.

**What would flip this:** deciding to pursue epiq in the browser as a product (shareable instances over a URL). Then the sandbox becomes a cheap, low-stakes way to force the core browser-portable — which is the first real chunk of that work. That is a strategic bet to make on its own merits, not to smuggle in as a demo.

## Findings worth keeping

**ghpages cannot host today's GUI.** It serves files; the GUI needs a Node process, a websocket and git subprocesses. A static demo would mean running the board entirely in the browser.

**The core is closer to portable than expected.** No node builtins in `event-boot.ts`, `event-materialize.ts`, `timeline-index.ts`, `api/issues.ts`, `api/issue-projection.ts`, `api/state.ts` (`getGuiState`), `state.ts` or `node-builder.ts`. `state.ts` touches the filesystem in exactly one place (lines 115-120, `resolveClosestEpiqProjectRoot` + `readProjectFile`) — an injection point, not a rewrite.

**Node-bound leaves:** `event-load.ts`, `event-persist.ts`, `log-signature.ts`, `storage/paths.ts`, `project-setup.ts`. `epiq-time-travel.ts` is node- and git-bound, but the part a demo needs — replaying the log to a moment — is on the pure side.

**The transport is the only seam.** The client speaks 33 websocket message types (`gui/api/lib/websocket.model.ts`) and knows nothing else about the server. A demo needs roughly ten of them; the rest can answer "not in the demo".

**Pre-baking:** the git-backed views (`commits:get`, `commit:diff:get`, `issue:commits:get`) are fixed for a fixed demo repo, so they can ship as JSON rather than be computed.

## Constraints any future attempt must respect

- **Seed data must be synthetic.** Exporting the real board would publish contributor names, emails and internal ticket text to a public, cached, hard-to-retract site.
- **Drift is the real risk.** Run the existing Playwright suite against the static build in CI, so divergence fails a job instead of shipping.
- **Isolation, if built:** `sandbox/` at the repo root rather than under `source/`, its own tsconfig with a DOM-only lib (the mechanism already enforcing the GUI client's node boundary via `build:gui:types`), and `no-restricted-imports` in both directions — `source/**` never imports `sandbox/**`, and `sandbox/**` never imports the node-bound leaves. No new eslint dependency needed. Deleting `sandbox/` plus one CI step must leave a green build, and that should be asserted by a test rather than intended.

The hosted-server alternative was explored and rejected earlier still — see `R2KHXNW`, also iceboxed, for the four changes it would need and why the security and cost profile is worse.

add.issue.name: Trim the Stats tab, drop coverage from it, and link every path into its diff

edit.description.md:
Follow-up to `P4W87ZD` after seeing the tab in use: too many numbers, too little hierarchy, and every path on it was a dead end.

**Trimmed.** Lines +/- is already the Commits tab's job, so the change is files · directories · concentration. "Touched a test — yes" becomes the count of test files added, which says the same thing and says more. The explanatory paragraphs under each section are gone: a stat that needs a paragraph is not a stat.

**Coverage removed entirely** — the section, `patch-coverage.ts`, `coverage-report.ts`, the `.epiq/stats.json` reading, the blame anchoring and their tests. It goes back when `VKN2ACF` settles whether and how a measurement is persisted; until then a number that silently means "the last time somebody ran the tests here" is worth less than no number. Restore from `4c1af752` and `2f20efe7`. Dropping it also takes the blame call out of the request, so the tab answers in tens of milliseconds, and the cache key goes back to being just the shas.

**Hierarchy.** The figure is 30px, its label 9px, its working 10px, each stat centred in its own column. Nothing else on the page competes with a number.

**Every path is a link into that file's diff.** The largest file, each test file added or deleted, the file the deepest nesting is in, and each flagged path: clicking one opens the Commits tab with that file expanded. `FilePointer` (path + the last of the ticket's commits to touch it) carries it through the payload, and `writeFileFocusParams` puts it in the URL, so the link survives a reload and can be handed to somebody else.

add.issue.comment.md:

add.issue.name: A command system for the GUI, with a command palette over it

edit.description.md:
The TUI has a command line and a `?` palette; the GUI has none, so every action is reachable only by finding the right button. That is what makes a board feel slow once you know it, and it is the bar Linear sets for a keyboard-first board.

A general command layer, not just a palette UI: a declarative registry plus a dispatcher, with the palette as the first surface over it. `Cmd/Ctrl+K`, fuzzy match, keyboard-first, recent commands remembered in localStorage.

## Sharing with the TUI: the vocabulary, not the machinery

`cmd-keywords.ts` has zero imports and is safe for the client. Everything around it is not: `command-intent.ts`, `command-meta.ts` and `command-parser.ts` all reach `state/state.js` → `project-setup.ts` → `node:fs`, and the client tsconfig (`lib: [ESNext, DOM]`, no `types`) fails the build on a node import. `commands.ts` also imports `export/export.js`, which imports `ink`.

The TUI palette itself is not a model to copy either — it builds virtual `NavNode`s against `nodeRepo`, which the GUI has no equivalent of. What carries across is its behaviour: match the command name by prefix and the description by substring past two characters, and sort unavailable commands last rather than hiding them.

So `CmdKeywords` is the single source of truth for command *names*, and the GUI writes its own registry of implementations. A unit test asserts every non-`gui:` command id is a real `CmdKeywords` value, which keeps the two vocabularies honest without coupling them.

## Shape

`lib/commands/` — `command.model.ts` (id, title, group, `isAvailable(ctx)`, `run(ctx)`, optional `getArguments(ctx)`), `command-context.model.ts`, `command-registry.ts` built from injected handlers so nothing reaches into a hook, `command-match.ts` (pure ranking), `command-recents.ts` (capped MRU in localStorage).

Commands adapted rather than transplanted. Direct: `new`, `delete`, `tag`, `untag`, `assign`, `unassign`, `close`, `reopen`, `comment`, `sync`, `filter`, `yank` (copy the ref), `replay` (opens the existing Theatre player). GUI-native where the TUI equivalent means nothing in a browser: toggle the log panel, toggle series, switch board view, return to live. Dropped: `exit`, `init`, `config`, `move`.

**Two-stage commands matter.** `tag`, `untag`, `assign`, `unassign` and `filter` take an argument, and a palette that can only fire argument-less commands is half a palette. `getArguments(ctx)` returns a list and the palette pushes a second step using the same matcher.

## Reuse rather than reimplement

Existing handlers are called, not rebuilt: `useIssueMutations`, `useSwimlaneEditing`, `useTheatrePlayback`, `useBoardSelection`, and `sendSocketJson` for the rest. The overlay follows `CreateNodeModal.tsx`; localStorage follows `use-persisted-flag.ts`'s guarded-read conventions; `mutation-gate.ts` decides what is unavailable while time-travelling, so a command does not fire into a 409.

No global key listener exists at App level today, so `Cmd/Ctrl+K` is free.

Nothing under `source/lib` changes, so the TUI is untouched — to be confirmed with the container suites rather than assumed.

add.issue.name: Comments are the part worth reading: yellow in the diff, and on the stats bar

edit.description.md:
Two halves of one idea, plus a stat that had to go.

**The diff paints comments bright yellow.** Every editor theme greys them out, on the premise that a comment is not the code. That is backwards for reading somebody else's change: the comment is the only part of a diff that says *why*, and it is what a reviewer most wants to find. `lib/diff-theme.ts` registers github-dark with every `comment*` scope repainted `#ffd479`; the Commits tab and quoted snippets both use it.

**The Stats tab's comment bar wears the same yellow**, with the code it explains in blue — so the bar and the file agree about which half is prose. The pair validates on this panel's surface (ΔE 27.4 protan, 30.7 normal), and the repo-baseline mark is now a slot cut through the bar in the panel colour rather than a grey line that vanished on blue.

**Test lines per code line is gone**, and the green bar under it with it. It says more about how a language is written than about whether a change is tested, and there is nothing a reader can do with it. What replaces it is test *lines* added, which keeps the case a ratio would have hidden: a ticket that adds forty lines to an existing test file used to read as "0 test files added".

Also: "The change" is now "Code".

add.issue.name: A Board section on the Stats tab, and less furniture around the figures

edit.description.md:
Three trims and one addition.

**Board stats.** Days old, times sent back, and days in the lane it is in now — the first of `WF435EW`'s Tier 1 to actually land. Derived in `lib/stats/board-stats.ts`, pure, from the ticket's own history: types in, numbers out, so the TUI and the MCP can each derive the same answer from their own copy of the log.

"Sent back" needed the log to say *where* a move went, which it only said in prose. `ApiIssueHistoryEntry` now carries `parentId` on move events, and the count is moves to a lane earlier in the board's order. A move to a lane the board does not have — closing a ticket, which moves it to another board entirely — counts as neither forwards nor back.

It renders last, being the only section not about the diff, and it is the one section that survives a ticket with no commits. That case used to render nothing at all, which was backwards: how long a ticket has sat is the *whole* story of one nobody has started.

**Notes removed** where the label already said it: "in files that already existed", "1 commit" under Directories, and the author's name under the author count.

**Thinner bars**, 8px to 4px. At 8 they read as blocks competing with the figures above them; at 4 they read as a measure beside them.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: a declarative command registry in `gui/client/lib/commands/`, with the palette as the first surface over it. Commands are `{id, title, group, unavailable(ctx), run(ctx)}` built from injected handlers, so the whole registry is a value the tests construct without a React tree.

`cmd-keywords.ts` turned out to be the only module pure enough for the client — zero imports. `command-intent`, `command-meta` and `command-parser` all reach `state/state.js` → `project-setup.ts` → `node:fs`, which fails `build:gui:types` under the client's DOM-only tsconfig, and `commands.ts` imports `export/export.js` → `ink`. So the GUI shares the *vocabulary* and writes its own implementations, with a unit test failing if any non-`gui:` id is not a real `CmdKeywords` value.

Two-stage commands carry the weight: `tag`, `untag`, `assign`, `unassign` and search push a second step through the same matcher, with Escape and Backspace-on-empty each popping one step.

Three things the work turned up that were not in the plan:

- **`delete` is absent.** The GUI has no `issue:delete` message at all, and inventing a destructive path with no confirmation UI was out of scope. `init`, `config`, `exit` and `move` are dropped as meaningless in a browser.
- **Adding a tag on a board with no tags** opened an empty list and no way forward. `addIssueTag` creates by name — the same reason `:tag urgent` works in the TUI — so the second step now offers a name the board has never held.
- **Search is project-wide**, not the board's text filter, and `openIssueTab` hardcoded the current board slug, so a hit on another board built a URL that would not resolve. Tickets carry `boardRef` and the handler takes an optional board override; every other caller is untouched.

Performance, for a project holding thousands of tickets: rows are capped at 50 *after* ranking, so what survives is the best of the whole set rather than the first 50 scanned — there is a test over 5,000 items whose target is last in the input. The argument list is memoized on the step and query alone, so it re-ranks when somebody types rather than on every board broadcast; a needle drag makes one of those every 120ms.

`Cmd/Ctrl+K` or a bare `:` opens it, the latter carrying the TUI's own way in. `?` is deliberately not a second door: on the web it means "show the keyboard shortcuts", and spending it here would cost that and buy nothing. A topbar hint teaches the chord as two keycaps, since `⌘` and `K` set solid read as one strange word.

Nothing under `source/lib` changed, so the TUI is untouched — confirmed by the container suites rather than assumed.

Merged to main as `0a097c24` and `4b7829b5` via PR #263 (rebase, both ref-prefixed). Gate green on the rebased base: lint, typecheck, 1337 unit, containers (17 e2e, 15 collaboration), 150 GUI browser — 11 of them new.

add.issue.name: Unvalidated commit sha reaches git argv and a file path: arbitrary file write from the GUI socket

edit.description.md:
Found by an adversarial read of `main` at `bf113210`. **This is the one to fix first.**

`commit:inspect` and `commit:diff:get` declare `sha: z.string()` (`gui/api/lib/websocket.schema.ts:118-119`) — any string at all. That value reaches git's argv and a filesystem path without ever being checked for the shape of a sha.

**Argument injection.** `execGit` uses `spawn` with no shell, so there is no shell injection — but a value starting with `-` is read by git as a *flag*, and `git show` accepts the diff machinery's options:

- `epiq-time-travel.ts:394` — `execGit({args: ['show', sha]})`. `sha = "--output=/Users/<you>/.zshenv"` makes git write its output to that path. A file written to a shell rc or a git hook is code execution the next time either runs.
- `epiq-time-travel.ts:440` — `['diff', '--name-only', `${sha}~1`, sha]`. The bare trailing `sha` is the same hole.
- `epiq-time-travel.ts:622` — `['diff', '--raw', '--numstat', ..., `${sha}~1`, sha]`. Same.

**Path traversal, in the same value.** `epiq-time-travel.ts:398-400` builds `path.join(os.tmpdir(), 'epiq', 'commit-diffs', `${sha}.diff`)` and writes to it. `sha = "../../../../Users/<you>/.zshenv"` writes there directly — no git flag needed.

**Reachability.** The origin guard correctly refuses a cross-origin browser page, including on the websocket handshake. But a request with no `Origin` is deliberately allowed (`origin-guard.ts:25` — "not coming from a page and has nothing to spoof"), which is right for curl and the test harness and means any *local* process can drive the socket. That is an accepted boundary for a loopback tool; what is not acceptable is that crossing it hands out file writes as the user rather than board edits.

**Fix**: constrain the sha at the schema boundary to what a sha can be — `/^[0-9a-f]{7,40}$/` — so the wire cannot carry anything else, and validate again at the API boundary rather than trusting the caller, since the MCP path reaches the same functions. Pass `--` before revisions where git accepts one, and stop interpolating the sha into a filesystem path; a hash of it, or a fixed name per request, does the same job.

Regression tests should be red without the fix: a `--output=` sha, a traversal sha, and a valid sha still working.

add.issue.name: Uncapped text on the GUI socket bloats the append-only log permanently

edit.description.md:
Found by an adversarial read of `main` at `bf113210`.

The websocket schema takes `title`, `description`, `body` and `tagName` as bare `z.string()` with no maximum (`gui/api/lib/websocket.schema.ts`), and `WebSocketServer` is constructed without `maxPayload` (`gui/api/lib/websocket.ts:149`), so `ws` allows its default 100 MB per frame.

The MCP guards the same fields — `epiq_issue_comment_add` caps a body at 4,000 and `epiq_issue_description_edit` a description at 20,000. The GUI socket is the unguarded door to the same log.

**Why this is worse than an ordinary size limit.** The event log is append-only and replicated. A 100 MB description is written as a line in a per-user JSONL file, committed to the state branch, pushed to the remote, and pulled by every clone. Deleting the ticket writes a *tombstone* — the bytes stay, because time travel has to be able to resolve the log at any earlier moment. Every future boot replays them: `mcp/api/boot.ts` already notes a twenty-person decade costing 169 MB and about eight seconds, and that is with everyone behaving.

So a single oversized frame is not a transient DoS. It is permanent, it replicates, and undoing it means history surgery on a branch the project treats as the system of record — which the epiq skill explicitly forbids editing by hand.

It does not take malice, either: a paste of a large log or a base64 blob into a description reaches the same place.

**Fix**: cap the text fields in the schema at the limits the MCP already uses, so the two doors to the log agree, and set `maxPayload` on the server as a backstop for every message at once rather than field by field. Both belong at the boundary — refusing the frame is the point, not truncating it after it has been parsed.

Worth deciding while fixing: whether an over-long field is refused with a message the GUI can show, or silently truncated. Refusing is more honest; the client should say so rather than appearing to save.

add.issue.name: Commit diffs are written to a predictable path in the shared temp directory

edit.description.md:
Found by an adversarial read of `main` at `bf113210`.

Opening a commit as a unified diff writes it to `os.tmpdir()/epiq/commit-diffs/<sha>.diff` (`mcp/epiq-time-travel.ts:398-400`) with default permissions and a fully predictable name.

Two consequences on a machine where `/tmp` is shared between users, which is the Linux default:

- **Disclosure.** Any local user can read the diffs of a private repository as they are written, and the filename tells them which commit to wait for.
- **Symlink redirection.** Another user can pre-create `epiq/commit-diffs/<sha>.diff` as a symlink to a file the epiq user can write. The write then lands on the target instead — a variant of the same file-write primitive `HE2XDRF` covers, reached without any malformed input.

macOS is milder: `os.tmpdir()` there is a per-user `/var/folders/...` path, so the neighbour is not present. Linux and any shared build machine are the exposure, and epiq ships Linux binaries.

**Fix**: create the directory with `0700` and, better, use a per-run directory from `fs.mkdtemp` rather than a fixed shared one, so the name cannot be guessed ahead of the write. `fileManager.mkDir` is the place to look first — if it can take a mode, everything using it benefits.

Lower priority than the other two: it needs a hostile local user rather than any local process, and the platform epiq is most used on is not the vulnerable one. Worth fixing while the surrounding code is open for `HE2XDRF`, since the offending path is built three lines from that fix.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution: withdrawn — not a bug. I filed this from the schema without tracing the value to where it is used, and the trace disproves it.

`sha` is validated before it reaches git. `epiq-time-travel.ts:387` defines `isPlausibleSha` as `/^[0-9a-f]{7,40}$/i`, and both exported entry points check it as their first statement: `openCommitDiffInEditor` (line 540) and `getCommitDiff` (line 700). The websocket handlers for `commit:inspect` and `commit:diff:get` call exactly those two (`websocket.ts:218`, `:236`).

Every helper I named — `openCommitAsUnifiedDiff`, `openCommitAsSideBySideDiffs`, `getChangedFilePaths`, `readFileAtRevision`, `getChangedFileBlobs` — is module-private and reachable only through those two guarded entry points. So neither the `--output=` argument injection nor the `../..` path traversal is reachable: a sha that could express either is refused before any of it runs.

The other two git call sites are clean as well. `getCommitTimeline` builds `--since=@<n>` from `Math.floor(start / 1000)` where `start` is already a finite number, and a number cannot express a flag. `getCommitsForRef` length-checks the ref and never reaches git — it filters an in-memory timeline.

What is left is not a vulnerability but a defence-in-depth observation, and a weak one: the wire schema says `z.string()` and the real constraint lives a layer in. That is a deliberate and reasonable division — the MCP reaches the same functions and gets the same guard, which would not be true if the check lived only in the schema. Tightening the schema would document the contract at the boundary, nothing more.

Closing as invalid rather than leaving a prio-1 on the board that describes a hole that is not there.

add.issue.comment.md:
Correction: the central claim here is wrong, and the ticket is being narrowed to what survives.

The log cannot be bloated this way. `lib/utils/text.limits.ts` defines `MAX_TITLE_LENGTH` 300, `MAX_DESCRIPTION_LENGTH` 20,000 and `MAX_COMMENT_LENGTH` 4,000, and the API layer enforces them — `api/comments.ts:46` and `:190` for comment bodies, `api/issues.ts:272-273` for title and description. The websocket handlers call those same functions, so an oversized field is refused before an event is written. The MCP and the GUI already agree; I claimed they did not because I read the wire schema and stopped there instead of following the value to the code that acts on it.

So there is no permanent log bloat, no replication of it, and no history surgery to undo it. That was the whole weight of the ticket and it is not real.

What does survive, much smaller: `WebSocketServer` is still constructed without `maxPayload` (`websocket.ts:149`), so `ws` allows its default 100 MiB per frame. A frame that large is fully buffered and then `JSON.parse`d before any handler — and therefore before the caps above get a say. The cost is transient memory in the GUI server, several times the frame size once parsed, from any local process that can reach the socket. It is a denial of service against a loopback dev tool, not corruption and not persistence.

Retitled and dropped to prio-3 accordingly. The fix is one option on the server rather than field-by-field schema work: a ceiling comfortably above the largest legitimate message — an attachment upload goes over HTTP, not this socket — so an absurd frame is refused at the transport instead of being parsed to find out it was absurd.

add.issue.name: A failed rebase --abort is indistinguishable from having nothing to abort

edit.description.md:
Found while adversarially reading the sync/merge path on `main` at `bf113210`. The rest of that path held up — this is the one gap worth recording.

`abortRebaseIfPresent` (`git/git-utils.ts:552-565`) runs `git rebase --abort` through `execGitAllowFail` and reads only the exit code: zero means "aborted a stale rebase", anything else means "no rebase to abort". Those are not the same thing. `git rebase --abort` also exits non-zero when there *was* a rebase and it could not be unwound — a corrupt `rebase-merge` directory, a permissions problem, an unreadable ORIG_HEAD.

In that case `pullBranchRebaseIfPresent` carries on to fetch and rebase over a worktree still mid-rebase, and the failure surfaces later as a confusing "Failed during rebase" naming the new rebase rather than the stuck one underneath it.

This is a diagnosability gap, not data loss. The integrity guards still hold: `withEventLogsIntact` restores lines git dropped, and `assertLogOnlyGrew` refuses to commit a log that shrank, so a wedged worktree cannot publish damage. What it costs is the operator's time — the message points at the wrong rebase, and the real cause is a directory nobody is told about.

**Fix**: tell the two apart. `git rebase --abort` fails with a recognisable message when there is no rebase in progress; anything else is a real failure and should be returned as one, so the caller stops instead of layering a second rebase on top. Worth checking `execGitAllowFail`'s stderr rather than inventing a state file.

add.issue.name: A write landing between autostash and checkout fails the sync, and CI never runs the suite that catches it

edit.description.md:
Pre-existing on `main` at `bf113210`. Found while gating unrelated hardening work — not caused by it, and verified so: reverting the only sync-path file that work touched (`git/git-utils.ts`) to main's version leaves the test failing identically.

`source/test/e2e-collab/write-during-sync.test.ts` → "keeps issues written into the same log file a sync is rewriting" fails deterministically here, twice out of two runs:

```
sync: Failed during rebase
git -c rebase.autoStash=true rebase origin/epiq/state
error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout:
	.epiq/events/<ulid>.ana.jsonl
Please commit your changes or stash them before you switch branches.
Aborting
error: could not detach HEAD
```

`rebase.autoStash` stashes the working copy and puts it back, but the window between the stash and the checkout is not covered: a write that lands inside it leaves the file dirty again, and the rebase then refuses to detach HEAD. The test's own header describes exactly this arrangement — a GUI beside an MCP server beside a TUI, only one of them syncing — and calls it "the ordinary arrangement for an agent-driven board".

The data contract still holds. `withEventLogsIntact` restores lines git dropped and `assertLogOnlyGrew` refuses to commit a shrunken log, so nothing is lost or published damaged. What fails is the sync itself, and the test asserts a clean sync — so this is a liveness problem, not a correctness one: the board stops publishing until the writer goes quiet.

**CI cannot see this.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `lint:err`, `build`, `test`, `test:e2e:ci` and `test:gui:ci`. It never runs `test:collab`. The collaboration suite exists only in the local pre-push gate, so a failure here blocks whoever pushes next and is invisible to everyone else — including on every PR merged since it started failing.

Two things worth deciding separately:

1. **The bug.** Retrying the rebase is the obvious move, since the condition is transient by construction, but a retry loop against a directory other processes are writing to needs a bound and a reason to believe the next attempt is likelier to win.
2. **The blind spot.** A suite that only ever runs on a developer's machine, as a push blocker, is one nobody sees fail until it is in their way. Either CI runs it or its absence is a deliberate, recorded decision — this ticket is the place to record which.

Filed rather than fixed: it is a distributed-systems change on the sync path, which is not something to fold into an unrelated branch.

add.issue.comment.md:
Solution (the bug half): a rebase that never started is re-attempted, up to three times, 120ms apart — `rebaseWithRetry` in `git/git-utils.ts`, merged as `f1c1fdc4` via PR #274.

The two failures are told apart structurally, reusing what `Y3ZKM2D` added rather than reading git's message — `gitEnv` inherits `LANG`, so the wording is not ours to rely on. A rebase that *stopped on a conflict* left its state directory behind and replaying it would land in the same place; one that *never started* left nothing, and the next attempt is a fresh throw against a window a few milliseconds wide.

That same test keeps the 120-second slow timeout from multiplying: a rebase SIGTERMed at the cap leaves `rebase-merge` like any interrupted one, so it reads as started and is not re-attempted. Only a rebase that cost nothing is paid for again.

`write-during-sync.test.ts` is the regression test and needed no changes — it was red twice out of two runs before, green after, and the file's runtime dropped from 154s to 85s as fewer sync rounds fail. Full gate green on the rebased base: 1368 unit, 17 e2e, **15/15 collaboration** (was 14/15), 150 GUI.

Three attempts is a judgement, not a proof. Under sustained write pressure all three can still lose, and the sync then fails as before — 240ms later. That is acceptable because autosync comes round again; the fix turns "fails often" into "fails rarely", it does not make the window disappear. Closing that properly would mean holding a lock across the write path, which is a much larger change than this one.

**Left open deliberately: the second half.** CI runs `lint:err`, `build`, `test`, `test:e2e:ci` and `test:gui:ci` — never `test:collab`. The collaboration suite is a local push blocker and nothing else, which is exactly why this sat broken invisibly on main and blocked the next person to push. Wiring it into CI means docker and minutes per PR; that is a cost decision for the user, not something to settle inside a fix. Reopening this ticket to that question rather than closing it as done.

add.issue.name: Writes made during a sync can be destroyed by it — accepted issues go missing

edit.description.md:
**Pre-existing on main. Reproduced with evidence, not inferred.** This is data loss, not a sync blip, and it contradicts what I said earlier on `V8TZ5CD` — I claimed correctness held there and that was wrong.

## What happens

`write-during-sync.test.ts` runs the ordinary arrangement — one tool appending while another syncs the same worktree — and issues the board *accepted* are afterwards missing from the machine that created them.

Measured on the same machine, same suite, only `git/git-utils.ts` differing:

| Version | Issues lost | Syncs blocked |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-hardening (`bf113210`) | **16** | 6 |
| With the `V8TZ5CD` retry | **2** | under 4 |

So the retry helps a great deal and is not the cause — but it does not fix this, and 2 is not 0.

## Why it was invisible

The test asserted zero sync problems *before* it asserted no missing issues. Under contention the sync assertion always failed first and aborted the test, so the data check was never reached. The suite has been failing for a shallow reason while hiding a deeper one — and `test:collab` does not run in CI, so nobody saw either.

It only surfaced because the sync assertion was relaxed (per the decision on `V8TZ5CD`) to let the run continue.

## Mechanism

`withEventLogsIntact` snapshots the logs at the start of a sync and restores lines git dropped at the end. `log-integrity.ts` is explicit that this "is not a lock. It is the weaker guarantee that whatever was already on disk is still on disk when git is done."

That guarantee has a hole exactly where this test aims: a line appended *after* the snapshot is not in it, so when `rebase --abort` or the autostash restore resets the worktree over it, there is nothing to put back. The protection covers writes that predate the sync, not writes that race it.

`assertLogOnlyGrew` does not catch it either — it compares against the same snapshot.

## Why this is prio-1

An issue the board said it created is gone from the machine that created it, with no error shown to whoever created it. This is the one contract the event log exists to keep, and the epiq skill's own words for the state branch apply: history corrupted this way "can corrupt history in ways no later fix can undo".

It needs a real fix, not a wider retry. The candidates are the two already named on `V8TZ5CD` — exclude writers for the duration of a sync, or make the restore cover lines that arrived mid-sync (re-snapshot before each destructive git step, rather than once at the top). The second looks smaller and is worth costing first.

Filed rather than fixed: the decision on `V8TZ5CD` was taken on my incorrect assurance that no data was at risk, so this needs to go back to the user before anyone picks a direction.

add.issue.comment.md:
Design, before any code on the append path. Two things ruled the shape.

**Re-snapshotting does not work, and is reverted.** Measured: 16 lost at baseline, 2 with the retry, 6 with per-step re-snapshot — the last is noise against the second. The reason is structural: the uncovered window is *during* the git call, not before it. A line written while git runs is in no snapshot and is gone from disk afterwards, so the restore has nothing to detect and nothing to put back. Snapshotting can only recover what it already saw.

**Untracked files survive.** `write-during-sync.test.ts` says it itself — "an untracked file is not what a rebase or an autostash touches". The loss happens because the log is *tracked*: git resets it. That is the lever.

## Shape

Writes go to `<userId>.<userName>.pending.jsonl` beside the real log, never staged and therefore never tracked. Git resets around it. A flush folds it into the tracked log under the sync lock, once git is done.

Why this beats a spill directory outside the worktree: every reader already globs `*.jsonl` in the events dir, so the pending file is picked up with no change to the read path. That matters more than it sounds — `mintEventId` derives the causal parent through `getEdgeRef`, which reads that directory. A spill the edge computation could not see would mint ids sorting before their own parent, which the architecture forbids outright. Keeping the pending file in the same directory makes the read path correct by construction rather than by remembering to union in four places.

## Flush, and why it is safe to duplicate

Ordering is append-then-remove, never remove-then-append: a crash between them leaves lines in both files, and `getSortedEvents` dedupes by id, so duplication is free. Loss is not.

Concurrent appends are handled by rotating rather than truncating — rename `X.pending.jsonl` to a unique name, append that file's lines to the tracked log, delete it. A writer appending during the rename lands in a fresh pending file at the original path and is not lost; rename is atomic. A crash mid-flush leaves a rotated file, so the flush picks up strays first.

## Interactions found while designing, each needing care

- **Filename parsing.** Identity comes from the file name, so the `.pending` marker has to be stripped where `EventFileNameSchema` parses it, or every pending event is attributed to a contributor called `<name>.pending`.
- **`assertLogOnlyGrew`.** It refuses a log that shrank. A pending file legitimately goes to zero on flush, so it must be excluded from that check — otherwise the guard against real damage starts firing on normal operation, which is worse than not having it.
- **Staging.** `stageStateBranchOwnEventFile` names one file, so pending is never committed. No change needed, but it is the reason the scheme holds.
- **`findStrandedEventLogs`.** Counts any `.jsonl` as worth saving; a pending file qualifies, which is correct.

## What it does not fix

A sync can still fail — the rebase races the same writer. That stays as it is, per the decision on `V8TZ5CD`: a failed sync retries, a failed write does not. This ticket is only about the write surviving.

## Handoff for review (1/2): the change

Branch `hardening-prio3`. Read this before the diff — the reasoning matters more than the code.

### The bug

An append lands in a file git tracks. To rebase, git stashes the working copy, checks out the remote's version and puts the stash back — a line written while that happens was in no stash, and the checkout writes over it. Issues the board *accepted* go missing from the machine that created them, with no error shown.

It is not a merge or CRDT flaw. `*.jsonl merge=union` handles concurrent appends correctly, but only for lines that are **committed**. An uncommitted line is invisible to the merge.

### The fix

Appends go to `<id>~pending.<name>.jsonl` beside the tracked log. Git does not track it, so a reset goes around it. A sync folds it in once git is done with the worktree.

Three decisions worth checking:

1. **The marker is on the id segment, not a `.pending` suffix.** Names can contain dots (`"J. Lampa"` → `<id>.j.-lampa`), so a suffix would be indistinguishable from a contributor called "pending". `sanitizeFilePart` maps everything outside `[a-z0-9._-]` to `-`, so no real id can contain `~`. **This is the load-bearing claim — please check it holds.**
2. **The name still ends in `.jsonl`.** Every reader globs for that, so the pending file is picked up with no read-path change. Not cosmetic: `mintEventId` derives an event's causal parent from that same directory, and an append it could not see would mint an id sorting before its own parent — which the architecture forbids outright.
3. **Rotate, append, delete — never truncate.** Renaming first means an append landing mid-flush creates a fresh file rather than being erased. Appending before deleting means a crash duplicates rather than loses, and dedupe-by-id makes duplicates free.

### Files

- `lib/event/pending-log.ts` — new; naming, and the flush.
- `lib/event/event-persist.ts` — `persist` writes to the pending log.
- `lib/event/event-load.ts` — strips the marker so the actor id resolves.
- `git/sync.ts`, `lib/project-setup/init-project.ts` — flush before staging.
- `git/git-storage.ts`, `git/git.ts` — a committed `.gitignore` so a pending log cannot be staged.
- `git/log-integrity.ts` — the snapshot skips pending logs.

### Not fixed, deliberately

A sync can still fail when it races a writer — per the decision on `V8TZ5CD`, a failed sync retries while a blocked write stalls a person. `61HAR6S`'s retry narrows those odds without closing them.

add.issue.name: Publishing a release makes it `latest` before its binaries exist, so install.sh 404s for the whole build

edit.description.md:
`install.sh` downloads `releases/latest/download/epiq-<os>-<arch>`. GitHub makes a release `latest` the moment it is published, but the tag push only then starts CI, and the binaries are uploaded five to ten minutes later. For that window the installer 404s with "no prebuilt binary for this platform".

Measured on v1.8.5: published 22:39:30, first asset uploaded 22:45:36 — six minutes broken.

The same gap is permanent when a Release job never runs: `release` and `release-macos-x64` both `needs: [test, gui]`, so a red GUI job leaves `latest` pointing at a release with no assets at all, forever (see the earlier note on skipped-not-failed Release jobs).

Fix, in two parts:

1. **CI holds the release out of `latest` until every binary is up.** A `release-hold` job with no `needs` marks the release a prerelease within seconds of the tag push; each upload re-asserts `prerelease: true`; a `release-publish` job gated on all five upload jobs clears the flag and sets `make_latest`. A failed upload therefore leaves `latest` on the last complete release rather than on a broken one. If the release was already a prerelease deliberately, the hold records that and the publish job stands down.

2. **`install.sh` never hard-fails on the residual race.** The `latest` fast path stays; when it 404s, fall back to the newest release in the API listing that actually carries this platform's asset, and say which version that is.
